---
title: "6. Neural networks from the inside"
subtitle: "Day 2 · 09:15–10:15 · Lecture + demo + lab"
---

Deep learning is built from one simple unit — the artificial neuron — repeated in layers. Its strength is learning useful features directly from raw images, sequences and text, so you don't have to design them by hand.

## The ideas, without the maths

- **Neuron:** multiply each input by a weight, add a bias, pass the sum through an activation function (e.g. ReLU or sigmoid).
- **Layers:** many neurons side by side; layers stacked one after another. Early layers in an image network detect edges and textures, later layers detect leaves, lesions and spots.
- **Training:** start with random weights, predict, measure the error, nudge every weight to reduce it (gradient descent with backpropagation). One pass through the training data is an **epoch**.
- **Overfitting brakes:** weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, early stopping.
- **Transfer learning:** reuse a network trained on millions of images or sequences and retrain only the last layer(s) on your data. This is how most biologists use deep learning.

## When to use deep learning

| Data | First choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Table of measurements (soil, weather, phenotypes) | Random forest or gradient boosting | Usually as good or better, with far less tuning |
| Images (leaves, drones, microscopy) | Pre-trained CNN or vision transformer | Learns visual features you couldn't hand-design |
| DNA, RNA or protein sequences | Pre-trained language model, or k-mer methods | Captures context and long-range patterns |
| Text (papers, field notes) | Pre-trained LLM | Language understanding comes built in |

## Live demo: Teachable Machine (10 minutes)

[Teachable Machine](https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com) trains an image classifier in the browser using transfer learning — no code.

1. Choose **Image project → Standard image model**.
2. Make two classes, e.g. *healthy leaf* and *damaged leaf*. Collect 20–30 webcam images of each, using real leaves or printed photos.
3. Click **Train model** and test it live.
4. Now break it: change the background, the lighting or the angle. Discuss why it fails — this sets up the "lab photos versus field photos" problem in Module 7.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Instructor notes
- Spend most of the hour on the demo and the overfitting plot; the lab code is short.
- Python uses scikit-learn's `MLPRegressor`; R uses `nnet` (one hidden layer). Both are fine for teaching the concepts. For real deep learning, Python users move to PyTorch or Keras, and R users to `torch` or `keras3`.
- The key message: neural networks are not automatically better. On tabular data, the random forest wins here.
:::
